title.en: The Three Brothers: The Spy-Glass, the Ship, and the Thief
title.zh: 三兄弟：千里鏡、造船與神偷

region.en: Ilocos region, northwestern Luzon, Philippines (narrator's home region)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋西北伊洛克斯地區（敘述者故鄉）

texts.period: Ilocano oral tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 12a 'The Three Brothers', eBook #8299

summary.en: A poor widow sends her three sons out for nine years of training. An-no learns glass-making and brings home a spy-glass in which all hidden things are visible; Berto becomes an expert boat-builder; the youngest falls in with robbers and becomes their most skillful member. With the glass the brothers locate the kidnapped Princess Amelia in a guarded island tower, Berto builds the ship, and Tito steals her out; when all three claim her, the king refuses the marriage and divides half his wealth equally among them.
summary.zh: 貧寡母遣三子外出九年學藝。長兄學製玻璃，攜回一窺千里、能見隱秘之物的千里鏡；次兄成造船巧匠；幼弟卻落入強盜之夥，練就全幫最精妙的偷技。三人憑千里鏡尋得被劫的阿梅莉亞公主，次兄造船，幼弟隻身入守衛森嚴的塔樓竊出公主。三位求娶者相持不下，國王索性不嫁，將半數家產均分三人。

sensitivity.note: Ilocano folktale recorded by Fansler from a Garcia narrator; archival record. Rival-Brothers type; Fansler compares Grimm No. 129 and Straparola VII, 5.

passages.text: There was once an old woman who had three sons; the father died when Tito, the youngest, was only five years old, and the good widow worked hard to bring them up. When her strength began to fail she called her sons before her: 'As you see my strength is failing me, I want each of you to go into the world to seek his fortune. After nine years, come back home and show me what you have learned to do.' At the crossroads where the wide road branched in three directions they agreed that An-no should take the north branch, Berto the south, and Tito the east, and that at the end of the nine years they should all meet there before presenting themselves to their mother.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 12 'The Three Brothers'; not verbatim.

passages.text: At the end of the nine years the three brothers met again at the place designated. An-no had been in the company of glass-makers and had learned the art of glass-making, bringing home a spy-glass in which everything hidden from the eyes of men could be seen; Berto had been employed in a shipyard and become an expert boat-builder; the youngest, unfortunately, had fallen into the company of notorious robbers, and while with this band had become the best and most skilful robber in the gang. Their mother was very glad to have all her sons with her once more.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 12 'The Three Brothers'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Shortly after the family was re-united, the king issued a proclamation stating that his daughter, the beautiful princess Amelia, had been kidnapped by a brave stranger, and that whoever could give any information about her and restore her to the palace should be allowed to marry her. An-no looked through his glass and saw her confined in a tower on an island; Berto built a ship, and when it was finished the three brothers sailed to the island — but the tower was so closely guarded by armed soldiers that it seemed impossible to get into it. 'Well, that is easy,' said Tito. 'You stay here and wait for my return. I will bring the princess with me.' Through his skill the famous young robber succeeded in rescuing her and bringing her to the ship, and the four sailed directly for the king's palace.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 12 'The Three Brothers'; not verbatim.

passages.text: With great joy the king received them, and a great feast was held in the palace in honor of the rescue of his daughter. After the feast the king asked the three brothers to which of them he should give his daughter's hand; each claimed the reward, and a quarrel arose among them. The king, seeing that all had played important parts in the rescue of the princess, decided not to bestow his daughter on any of them — instead, he gave half his wealth to be divided equally among An-no, Berto, and Tito.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 12 'The Three Brothers'; not verbatim.

title.en: Three Brothers of Fortune: The Book, the Mat, and the Magic Stones
title.zh: 三兄弟的運氣：神書、飛毯與魔石

region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋邦阿西楠省羅薩利斯（故事原鄉）

texts.period: Pangasinan oral tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 12b 'Three Brothers of Fortune', eBook #8299

summary.en: Three idle brothers skip school and wander abroad, buying a life-restoring book from an old woman, a flying mat from another, and finding two stones that unite things of the same kind. Ambo revives a drowned girl, Iloy flies the party to the seashore, and Suan mends their storm-wrecked boat with his stones. When all three claim the girl, the king's savage judgment divides her body three ways — and it is Suan, re-uniting the useless portions with his stones, who brings her back to life and marries her.
summary.zh: 三位遊手好閒的兄弟棄學出走：一人購得還魂書，一人購得飛行蓆，一人拾得能合併同類之物的雙石。安波救活溺水女子，伊洛伊以飛毯載眾至海濱，蘇安以魔石修補風暴中的破船。三人爭奪女子時，國王竟判將屍身三分——蘇安以石合其三份，女子復活，嫁蘇安而樂。

sensitivity.note: Pangasinan folktale recorded by Fansler from an Estayo narrator (story heard from a native of Rosales); archival record. The dismemberment judgment is garbled (Fansler notes it as 'inhuman') — retained as recorded; cf. Vetâlapancavinçati No. 2.

passages.text: In former times there lived in a certain village a wealthy man who had three sons — Suan, Iloy, and Ambo. As this man was a lover of education, he sent all his boys to another town to school; but the three brothers did not study: they spent their time in idleness and extravagance. When vacation came they were ashamed to go back to their home town, so instead they wandered from town to town seeking their fortunes. In the course of their travels they met an old woman broken with age, who sold Ambo a book: 'If you want to restore a dead person to life, just open this book before him, and in an instant he will be revived.' Another old woman sold Iloy a mat: 'If you want to travel through the air, just step on it, and in an instant you will be where you desire to go.' Suan alone had no charm — until he saw two stones which would meet and unite to form one round black stone, and then separate again; believing they possessed magical power to unite things of the same or similar kind, he picked them up.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 12 'Three Brothers of Fortune'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Not long afterward they came upon a crowd of persons weeping over the dead body of a beautiful young lady. Ambo told the parents that he would restore her to life if they would pay him a reasonable sum; they gladly agreed, he opened his book, and the dead lady was brought back to life. As soon as he had received his reward, Iloy placed his mat on the ground, told his two brothers to hold the young woman, and stepped on the mat: in an instant all four were transported to the seashore. From there they took ship to another country; but when they were in the middle of the sea a severe storm came and their boat was wrecked — all on board would have been drowned had not Suan repaired the broken planks with his two magical stones.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 12 'Three Brothers of Fortune'; not verbatim.

passages.text: When they landed, a quarrel arose among the three brothers as to which one was entitled to the young woman. 'I am the one who should have her, for it was I who restored her to life,' said Ambo. 'But if it had not been for me, we should not have the lady with us,' said Iloy. 'And if it had not been for me, we should all be dead now, and nobody could have her,' said Suan. As they could not come to any agreement, they took the question before the king, who decided to divide the young woman into three parts to be distributed among the three brothers; his judgment was carried out. Iloy and Ambo were discontented because their portions were useless, so they threw them away; but Suan picked up the shares of his two brothers and united them with his own. The young woman was brought to life again, and lived happily with Suan — so, after all, Suan was the most fortunate.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 12 'Three Brothers of Fortune'; not verbatim.

title.en: Pablo and the Princess: The Carpet, the Book, and the Ivory Tube
title.zh: 帕布洛與公主：魔毯、奇書與象牙管

region.en: La Laguna, Luzon, Philippines (narrator's home province)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋內湖省（敘述者故鄉）

texts.period: Tagalog oral tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 12c 'Pablo and the Princess', eBook #8299

summary.en: Three friends take three roads and are each rewarded for their kindness: Pedro a transport carpet, Juan a book that knows everything happening in the world, Pablo an ivory tube that cures the dying. Juan's book reveals a dying princess, Pedro's carpet carries them to her, and Pablo's tube revives her — but when the king sets a shooting-match at the banana-flower that represents her heart, only Pablo refuses to shoot at it, for he loves her too dearly; and so he wins her.
summary.zh: 三位好友分道而行，各因善行得寶：佩德羅得可瞬間抵達任意之地的魔毯、胡安得知曉天下事的奇書、帕布洛得能起死回生的象牙管。書中傳來公主病危的消息，魔毯將三人送至王宮，象牙管救活公主。國王以香蕉花代表公主之心，令三人射箭定婚——只有帕布洛拒射：『我愛她太深。』於是公主屬於帕布洛。

sensitivity.note: Tagalog folktale recorded by Fansler from a Zafra narrator (La Laguna); archival record. Rival-suitors type with the arrow contest (cf. the 1001 Nights Prince Ahmed).

passages.text: Once upon a time there lived three friends, Pedro, Juan, and Pablo, who met one morning at the junction of three roads and agreed to each take one road and set out to find his fortune, promising to meet again in the same place, the first who came to wait for the others. Pedro took the road to the right: after three months' travelling he met an old man who asked him for food, and gave him his bread; in return the old man gave him a carpet — whoever sits on it may be transported instantly to any place he desires. Juan took the road to the left, and after three months and a half likewise shared his dinner-bread with a hungry old man, receiving a book by which he could read everything that was happening in the world at all times. Pablo took the middle road, and after travelling four months gave his bread to another old man, receiving an ivory tube that cures all sick persons of every disease — even a dying patient is restored instantly to perfect health if you blow through one end of the tube into his nose.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 12 'Pablo and the Princess'; not verbatim.

passages.text: At the crossroads they congratulated one another and exchanged fortunes. While Pedro was looking in Juan's book he read that a certain princess in a distant kingdom was very sick, and that the king her father had promised her hand and his heirship to whoever could cure her. They seated themselves on the carpet and were transported in a flash to the king's palace; led into the room of the sick princess, Pablo took his tube and blew through one end of it into her nose. She immediately opened her eyes, sat up, and began to talk.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 12 'Pablo and the Princess'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Before the king each claimed the princess: 'It is true, Pablo, that you are the one who cured my daughter; but could you have contrived to cure her if you had not known from Juan's book that she was sick, and if Pedro's carpet had not brought you here without delay? Your book, Juan, revealed that my daughter was sick; but the knowledge of her illness would have been of no service had it not been for Pedro's carpet and Pablo's tube. And it is just the same way with your carpet, Pedro.' Unable to choose among them, the king proposed a contest: 'Go and procure, each one of you, a bow and an arrow. I will hang up the inflorescence of a banana-plant. This will represent the heart of my daughter. The one who shoots it in the middle shall be the husband of my daughter, and the heir of my kingdom.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 12 'Pablo and the Princess'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Pedro shot first, and his arrow passed directly through the middle of the banana-flower; Juan shot second, and his arrow passed through the same hole Pedro's arrow had made. Now came Pablo's turn — but when Pablo's turn came, he refused to shoot, saying that if the banana-flower represented the heart of the princess, he could not shoot it, for he loved her too dearly. When the king heard this answer he said, 'Since Pablo really loves my daughter, while Pedro and Juan do not, for they shot at the flower that represents her heart, Pablo shall marry the princess.' And so Pablo married the king's daughter, and in time became king of that country.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 12 'Pablo and the Princess'; not verbatim.

title.en: Legend of Prince Oswaldo: The Old Man Who Was the Capitalist
title.zh: 奧斯瓦爾多王子傳：自稱『出資人』的老人

region.en: Calamba, La Laguna, Luzon, Philippines (narrator's home town)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋內湖省卡蘭巴（敘述者故鄉）

texts.period: Tagalog oral legend; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 12d 'Legend of Prince Oswaldo', eBook #8299

summary.en: A groaning old man at the crossroads gives three youths a hundred pesos each and directs them to buy the first things they find sold: a rain-coat that carries its wearer anywhere, a book that tells all the world's happenings, a violet bottle that restores the dead. The book announces the death of the princess of Berengena; the coat carries all three there; Juan risks his head to revive her and wins her — until all three sue. An old man then claims none of them, as he was the capitalist: 'the interest is mine' — and marries her, becoming the young Prince Oswaldo the moment the sun rises, freed from enchantment by his marriage.
summary.zh: 十字路口呻吟的老人各賜百金，囑三青年買下路旁所售第一物：可任意飛行的雨衣、知曉天下事的奇書、能起死回生的紫色瓶。書中傳來貝倫赫納公主的死訊；雨衣攜三人瞬至靈堂；胡安以性命為注，將公主救活並求娶。三人相爭之際，一老人挺身而出：『你們誰也不能娶——是我指給你們寶物之路、給你們本錢，我是出資人，利息歸我。』他娶了公主；日出之光中，老人化作解除魔咒的年輕王子奧斯瓦爾多，登基為王。

sensitivity.note: Tagalog legend recorded by Fansler from an Uichanco narrator (Calamba); archival record. Rival-brothers type with an enchanted-prince resolution.

passages.text: Once upon a time, on a moonlight night, three young men were walking monotonously along a solitary country road, and when they came to a place where the road branched into three they stopped there like nails attracted by a powerful magnet. At this crossroads a helpless old man lay groaning as if in mortal pain; the three companions ran to him, helped him up, and fed him a part of the rice they had with them. He thanked them, gave each of the companions a hundred pesos, and said, 'Each one of you shall take one of these branch-roads. At the end of it is a house where they are selling something. With these hundred pesos that I am giving each of you, you shall buy the first thing that you see there.' Pedro, on the left branch, bought a rain-coat: 'It will take you wherever you wish to go.' Diego, on the middle road, bought a book: 'It will tell you what is going on in all parts of the world.' Juan, on the third road, bought a bottle of violet-colored liquid: 'It brings the dead back to life.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 12 'Legend of Prince Oswaldo'; not verbatim.

passages.text: When Diego opened his book he read what appeared on the page: 'The beautiful princess of Berengena is dead. Her parents, relatives, and friends grieve at her loss.' 'Good!' answered Juan. 'Then there is an occasion for us to test this bottle. It restores the dead back to life.' 'Then we shall have occasion to use my rain-coat,' said Pedro, and wrapping it about all three of them wished them in Berengena; within a few minutes they reached that country, where the princess was already in the church, her parents weeping over her and everybody wearing deep mourning. When the three strangers boldly entered the church the guard arrested them, for they had on red clothes; and when Juan protested that the princess was only sleeping, the king called him a fool — until Juan, staking his head, secured a formal agreement: success would win the princess and the heirship, failure the scaffold.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 12 'Legend of Prince Oswaldo'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Blinded by his love for the beautiful princess, Juan tremblingly uncorked his bottle of violet liquid and held it under the nose of the princess — an hour, hours, while the people grew impatient and the scaffold waited. 'Nameless stranger! upon your honor, tell us the truth! Can you do it, or not? Speak. I command it!' Just as Juan was about to reply, he saw the right hand of the princess move; soon she moved her other hand and opened her eyes, exclaiming, 'Oh, where am I?... No, there is my father, there is my mother, there is my brother.' The king was fully satisfied; he ordered Juan's clothes exchanged for prince's garments so that the celebration of the marriage might take place at once, and the people shouted, 'Long live Juan! Long live the princess!'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 12 'Legend of Prince Oswaldo'; not verbatim.

passages.text: When Diego and Pedro heard the shout they could not help feeling cheated, and made their way through the crowd: 'If it had not been for my book, we could not have known that the princess was dead... And Juan's good luck is due to my rain-coat.' The king was overwhelmed — each of the three had a good reason, but all three could not marry the princess, and even the counsellors could not decide. While they were puzzling over it, an old man sprang forth from the crowd and declared that he would settle the difficulty: 'None of you shall marry the princess. You, Juan, shall not marry her, because you intended to obtain your fortunes regardless of your companions; and you, Pedro and Diego, shall not have her, because you did not accept your misfortune quietly and thank God for it. None of you shall have her. I will marry her myself. I am the one who showed these three companions where to get their bottle, rain-coat, and book. I am the one who gave each of them a hundred pesos. I am the capitalist: the interest is mine.' The old man was right; the crowd clapped their hands, and the princess, bitterly weeping, gave her hand to the old man, who seemed to be her grandfather. But just then the sun began to rise, and the whole church was flooded with light: when the people recovered, they found their princess walking with her husband, not an old man, but a gallant young prince — none other than Prince Oswaldo, who had just been set free from the bonds of enchantment by his marriage. He was seated on the throne, the crown and sceptre were transferred to him, and he was hailed as King Oswaldo of Berengena.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 12 'Legend of Prince Oswaldo'; not verbatim.

title.en: The Rich and the Poor: The Ring in the Fat Fish
title.zh: 富者與貧者：肥魚腹中的戒指

region.en: Pasig and Laguna de Bay, Luzon, Philippines (story localized there)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋帕西格與內湖灣（故事發生地）

texts.period: Tagalog oral tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 13a 'The Rich and the Poor', eBook #8299

summary.en: Two friends wager which can make a poor wood-cutter rich. Mayaman's six gifts of money are stolen each time by dishonest neighbors, and his magic wish-ring is lost when its commanded wind sinks the banca — into the lake. Mahirap's five centavos buy the very fish whose belly holds the lost ring; talking aloud to it, the wood-cutter startles the thieves into returning every stolen bag, and he becomes the richest man in town.
summary.zh: 二友打賭誰能讓貧苦樵夫致富。富人梅雅曼六次贈金六次遭竊；他賜的許願戒指因一句『起風』弄沉小船而失落湖中。窮人馬希拉普僅以五仙買下一尾肥魚——魚腹中正是那枚戒指！樵夫捧戒高歌，竊金鄰人以為被識破，捧著全部贓物前來求恕。樵夫自此富甲全鎮。

sensitivity.note: Tagalog folktale recorded by Fansler from a Gomez narrator (Rizal); archival record. Localized on Laguna de Bay; Fansler connects it with the Arabian Nights 'Khevajah Hasan al-Habbal.'

passages.text: Once upon a time there lived in the town of Pasig two honest men who were intimate friends, called Mayaman and Mahirap because one was much richer than the other. One pleasant afternoon they took a long walk into the neighboring woods, and saw in the distance a poor wood-cutter busy cutting and collecting fagots for sale, who maintained his family by selling wood from the forest. 'Now, which one of us can make that wood-cutter rich?' said Mayaman. 'Well, even though I am much poorer than you,' said Mahirap, 'I can make him rich with just the few cents I have in my pocket.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 13 'The Rich and the Poor'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Mayaman tried first: evening after evening he gave the wood-cutter four bags of money, and six times the dishonest neighbors who found out that the wood-cutter had much money in the house secretly stole the bags. Finally, on his sixth application, Mayaman presented him with a beautiful ring instead: 'This ring will preserve you from harm, and will give you everything you ask for. With it you can become the richest man in town; but be careful not to lose it!' Sailing home, the wood-cutter asked it for food — twelve different kinds of food appeared in his banca — and then, the wind having calmed, he said to the ring, 'O beautiful ring! blow my banca very hard, so that I may reach home quickly.' The wind rose suddenly, the sail and mast were blown away, the banca sank, and the unfortunate man, swimming for his life, reached the shore to find he had lost his valuable ring.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 13 'The Rich and the Poor'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Mayaman had nothing more to give, so it was Mahirap's turn: he gave the poor wood-cutter five centavos, all he had in his pocket, and told him to go to the market and buy a fish with it for his supper. At the fish-stalls the wood-cutter saw a very fine fat fish and, unable to bargain it down, gave all his money for it. When he went home and opened the fish to clean it, what did he find inside but the precious ring he had lost in the lake! He was so rejoiced at getting back his treasure that he walked up and down the streets talking out loud to his ring — 'Ha, ha, ha, ha! I have found you now; you are here, and nowhere else.' When his neighbors who had stolen his bags of money heard these words, they thought the wood-cutter had found out they were the thieves and was addressing these words to them; they ran up to him with all the bags of money, saying, 'O wood-cutter! pardon us for our misdoings! Here are all the bags of money that we stole from you.' With his money and the ring, the wood-cutter soon became the richest man in his town — and so Mahirap, with five centavos only, succeeded in making the wood-cutter rich.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 13 'The Rich and the Poor'; not verbatim.

title.en: Lucas the Rope-Maker: The Lead That Was Worth Twenty Thousand Pesos
title.zh: 搓繩人盧卡斯：價值兩萬的鉛

region.en: Pagsanjan, La Laguna, Luzon, Philippines (story well known there, set in 'Bagdad')
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋內湖省帕桑漢（故事聞名之地，背景設於『巴格達』）

texts.period: Tagalog oral tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 13b 'Lucas the Rope-Maker', eBook #8299

summary.en: Kindhearted Luis twice gives his friend the rope-maker Lucas money, and twice it vanishes — an eagle snatching the hat with the second sum; even the third gift, a thousand pesos, is lost when his starving wife fills the money-jar with darak for the rice-seller. Given a piece of lead instead, Lucas lends it to a neighbor; the fish her husband catches holds a bright stone, which Lucas sells for twenty thousand pesos, becoming the kindliest rich man in town.
summary.zh: 仁厚的路易斯兩度贈金給搓繩人盧卡斯，兩度失散——鷹叼走藏錢的帽子；妻子又把藏千金的空甕裝滿豆麩償還米商。第三次，路易斯只給他一塊鉛：盧卡斯把鉛借給鄰婦作漁線墜，其夫釣回的大魚腹中藏一寶石——盧卡斯以兩萬比索售出，從此成為鎮上最仁厚的富翁。

sensitivity.note: Tagalog folktale recorded by Fansler from a Cordero narrator (Pagsanjan), who says the story is well known and old; archival record. Fansler derives it from the Arabian Nights 'History of Khevajah Hasan al-Habbal.'

passages.text: Luis and Isco were intimate friends in a country called Bagdad; Luis believed that gentleness and kindness were the second heaven, while Isco believed that wealth was the source of happiness. That afternoon they went to a town called Cohija, where they saw a rope-maker, Lucas by name, whose condition showed his great suffering from poverty; he had six little children to support but no money with which to feed them, nor could he get anything from his rope-making. Approaching Lucas, Luis gave him a roll of paper money, saying, 'Now, Lucas, take this money and spend it judiciously.' Lucas was overjoyed, hardly knowing what to do.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 13 'Lucas the Rope-Maker'; not verbatim.

passages.text: With his hundred pesos Lucas bought two pounds of meat and a roll of cañamo; but as he walked home an eagle, attracted by the smell of the meat, flew about his head and snatched off the hat in the corner of which he had put the leftover money — and when he searched, the money was gone. His wife Zelima scolded him roundly, and after the family had eaten the meat they were as poor as before, even pale because of hunger. Later, Luis and Isco found Lucas weeping under a mango-tree and, perceiving he told the truth, Luis gave him a thousand pesos; Lucas hid the bulk of the money in an empty jar in the corner of the room and went out to buy food — and while he was gone his starving wife, having nothing with which to repay the rice-seller who gave her rice, filled the jar with darak and gave it away. When Lucas came home and found the money gone he was in despair, and tried to kill himself, but his children prevented him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 13 'Lucas the Rope-Maker'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Two months later Luis and Isco again visited their friend, and Luis, who had found a big piece of lead in the street, gave it to Lucas, saying, 'Now, take care of that! Maybe your wealth will come from it.' Lucas accepted it unwillingly, thinking he was mocked, and threw the lead in the corner; but during the night a neighbor knocked at their door, asking for a piece of lead for her husband's fishing-line, and Zelima found the lead and gave it to her, receiving the promise of the first fish her husband should catch. The next morning the neighbor was there with a big fish, and while Zelima was cleaning it she found a bright stone inside it; ignorant of its value, she gave it to her youngest son to play with, and the children quarrelled over it. Don Juan, the rich man in front of whose house they lived, heard the noise of the quarrelling children, and his wife saw the stone and wanted it very much.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 13 'Lucas the Rope-Maker'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Don Juan offered the rope-maker a thousand pesos for the stone, but Lucas refused, for now he suspected it was worth more than that; at last he sold it for twenty thousand pesos. Lucas was now a rich man: he bought clothes for his wife and children, renewed his falling house, and bought a machine for making rope, then another; but although he was the richest man in town he was very kind — his house was open to every comer, he supported crippled persons, and gave alms to the poor. When Luis and Isco visited Lucas the last time they were surprised and delighted to see him so rich, and Lucas gave a banquet in honor of these two men, telling them every detail of all that had happened to him. Luis was now convinced that Lucas was honest, and had told the truth on former occasions; and Lucas lived in his big house happily and in peace with his wife and children.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 13 'Lucas the Rope-Maker'; not verbatim.

title.en: The King and the Dervish: Deer, Nightingale, and Dog
title.zh: 國王與苦行僧：鹿、夜鶯與犬

region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋八打雁省（敘述者故鄉）

texts.period: Tagalog oral tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 14a 'The King and the Dervish', eBook #8299

summary.en: A dervish who can leave his body and enter dead creatures teaches the king the charm; mid-hunt the dervish seizes the king's vacated body and orders the marked deer killed. The king flees through a nightingale's body into the palace cage, pecking the false king whenever he is touched; when the dervish leaves to revive the 'dead' bird, the king darts from the dog's body into his own and kills the ungrateful bird — and the queen dies of grief at learning she was deceived.
summary.zh: 能離體附身的苦行僧授國王咒術；狩獵之中，僧人趁虛入主王體，下令獵殺帶記號的鹿。真國王藉夜鶯之屍逃入王宮鳥籠，每被假王觸碰便啄之；待苦行僧離體去『救活』夜鶯，國王自犬身返回本體，手刃忘恩之鳥——而王后知曉被欺，悲傷而死。

sensitivity.note: Tagalog folktale recorded by Fansler from a Hilario narrator (Batangas); archival record. Fansler derives it from the 1001 Days story of Prince Fadlallah; the transformation requires a dead body to enter.

passages.text: Once there lived a young and brave king with his gentle and loving wife; he ruled his people well, and she always cheered her husband when he was sad. One day a dervish came to the palace and told the king that he possessed magical power, and straightway they became friends. This dervish had the power to leave his body and enter that of a dead animal or person. The king was fond of hunting, and once he took his new friend with him to shoot deer; after a few hours of hard chasing they succeeded in killing a buck, and to show his power the dervish left his body and entered that of the dead deer, then resumed his former shape.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 14 'The King and the Dervish'; not verbatim.

passages.text: The king was very anxious to be able to do the same thing; the dervish gave him minute instructions and taught him the necessary charms — and then the king left his body and took possession of that of the deer, while in an instant the dervish entered the king's body and went home as the monarch, giving orders that a deer with certain marks should be hunted out and killed. The true king was very unhappy, especially when he saw his own men chasing him to take his life.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 14 'The King and the Dervish'; not verbatim.

passages.text: In his wanderings through the forest he saw a dead nightingale, and left the deer's body and entered the bird's. Now he was safe, so he flew to his palace and sang so sweetly that the queen ordered her attendants to catch him; he gladly allowed himself to be caught and to be cared for by the queen. Whenever the dervish took the bird in his hands, the bird pecked him; but the beautiful singer always showed signs of satisfaction when the queen smoothed his plumage. Not long after the bird's capture, a dog died in the palace, and the king underwent another change, leaving the bird's body and entering that of the dog.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 14 'The King and the Dervish'; not verbatim.

passages.text: On waking up in the morning the queen found that her pet was dead, and began to weep; unable to see her so sad, the dervish comforted her and told her he would give the bird life again. Consequently he left the king's body and entered the bird's — and seeing his chance, the real king left the dog's body and resumed his original form, going at once to the cage and killing the ungrateful bird, the dervish. The tender queen protested against the king's act of cruelty; but when she heard that she had been deceived by the dervish, she died of grief.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 14 'The King and the Dervish'; not verbatim.

title.en: The Mysterious Book: The Transformation Chase

region.en: Calamba, La Laguna, Luzon, Philippines (narrator's home town)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋內湖省卡蘭巴（敘述者故鄉）

texts.period: Tagalog oral tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 14b 'The Mysterious Book', eBook #8299

summary.en: Idle Juan opens his master Don Luzano's seventh, gem-bound box and is carried into the air by the triangular gold book inside — pursued by his raging master. Whoever has touched the book can change into any form: steed against mule, bird against hawk, fish against fish hiding in a crack of the well — until the princesses of the well catch the seven-scaled fish. When Don Luzano, promising to cure the sick princess, demands her fish as payment, the fish becomes a gold ring, the ring a shower of mungo seeds, the crow that devours them is torn apart by the cat Juan has become — and Juan stands an embroidered prince beside his beloved.
summary.zh: 懶漢胡安開啟主人東·盧薩諾的第七重寶匣，被匣中金鑲鑽的三角奇書捲上天空——主人在後暴怒追趕。凡觸書者可任意變形：小馬對騾、小鳥對鷹、小魚對大魚躲入井壁裂縫——直到井邊三位公主釣起七彩鱗的小魚。東·盧薩諾假意醫病、索討公主之魚為酬；魚化金戒、戒化滿地豆粒、吞食豆粒的烏鴉被化貓的胡安撕裂——胡安以錦袍王子之姿站在所愛身旁。

sensitivity.note: Tagalog folktale recorded by Fansler from an Uichanco narrator (Calamba); archival record. Transformation-combat cycle; Fansler compares Grimm's 'The Thief and his Master' and Dasent's 'Farmer Weathersky,' tracing the family to India.

passages.text: Once upon a time there lived a poor father and a poor son — the father old, named Pedro; the son, Juan, afraid of work though they were very poor. One day, with not a single grain of rice in the house, Juan went to a neighboring town to seek a master, and found one in the person of Don Luzano, a fine gentleman of fortune. Don Luzano treated Juan like a son, and in time intrusted him with the most precious valuables in the house. One morning, going out hunting, he left Juan alone as usual; while Juan was sweeping and cleaning his master's room, he caught sight of a highly polished box lying behind the post in the corner.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 14 'The Mysterious Book'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Curious, Juan opened the box: there appeared another box; he opened this box and another box still was disclosed — one box after another until Juan came to the seventh, which contained a small triangular-shaped book bound in gold and decorated with diamonds and other precious gems. Disregarding the consequences, Juan picked up the book and opened it — and at once he was carried up into the air. When he looked back, whom did he see but Don Luzano pursuing him with eyes full of rage and an enormous deadly-looking bolo in his hand. The book had the wonderful power of changing anybody who had laid his hands on it into whatever form that person wished to assume: Juan became a little steed galloping down the street — Don Luzano a big fast mule with bubbling and foaming mouth; Juan a pretty little bird — Don Luzano a big hawk about to swoop down on him; then Juan suddenly leaped into a well he was flying over and became a little fish, Don Luzano assuming the form of a big fish — until the little fish entered a small crack in the wall of the well where the big fish could not pursue him farther, and Don Luzano had to give up and go home in great disappointment.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 14 'The Mysterious Book'; not verbatim.

passages.text: The well belonged to three beautiful princesses, and one morning while they were looking into the water they saw the little fish with its seven-colored scales moving gracefully through the water. The eldest lowered her bait, but the fish would not see it; the second sister tried her skill, but the fish released its hold just as it was being drawn out; the youngest sister's turn came, and the fish allowed itself to be caught and held in the tender hands of this beautiful girl, who placed it in a golden basin of water and cared for it very tenderly. Several months later the king issued a proclamation saying that the youngest princess was sick and promising half his kingdom to anyone who could cure her.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 14 'The Mysterious Book'; not verbatim.

passages.text: 'Ay, what foolishness!' exclaimed Don Luzano when he heard the news. 'The sickness! Pshaw! That's no sickness, never in the wide world!' — and the following morning he told the king he had already cured many similar cases, asking as token only the fish the princess kept in her room. On the third day, before beginning any part of the treatment, he requested that the fish be given him; but as he was about to dip his hand into the basin, the princess boldly stopped him, saying he would soil with his hands the golden basin of the monarch — she would pour the fish into his hands. Before the fish could reach them it jumped out; in its stead was a beautiful gold ring adorning the finger of the princess. Don Luzano tried to snatch the ring, but as the princess jerked her hand back the ring fell to the floor, and in its place were countless little mungo seeds scattered about the room. Don Luzano instantly took the form of a greedy crow, devouring the seeds with extraordinary speed — but Juan, contained in one of the seeds that had rolled beneath the feet of the princess, suddenly became a cat, and rushing out attacked the bird: as soon as you could wink your eyes, the crow was dead, miserably torn to pieces, and in place of the cat stood Juan in an embroidered suit, looking like a gay young prince. 'This is my beloved,' confessed the princess to her father; and the king forgave his daughter and gladly welcomed his new son-in-law — rid of his formidable antagonist, with a beautiful princess for a wife, and an excellent chance of inheriting the throne.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 14 'The Mysterious Book'; not verbatim.
